<tool-use data-tool-type="generic" data-tool-name="run_in_terminal"><details>
<summary>Tool use: **run_in_terminal**</summary>

**Input:**

- command: `cd /home/vinothkumars/openbmc_contribution/uuid/bmcweb && git log --format="%B" -1 | head -20`
- explanation: `See detailed commit message format`
- goal: `Understand commit description style`
- mode: `sync`

**Result:**

```
Fix Manager EventLog ClearLog Accept handling

The ClearLog action returns a JSON Redfish response, but it checks the
Accept header for application/octet-stream. This causes requests with
Accept: application/json to be marked as Bad Request.

The handler does not return after setting the error status, so it still
clears the log and returns a JSON success message. Remove the invalid
check to return the correct status.

Change-Id: Ica492e3185f970d39dd1655165ba623c5e7e29a4
Signed-off-by: Rex Fu <rex.fu@amd.com>

```
</details></tool-use>

```
Use type-safe enums for State and Health properties

Currently, several functions return State and Health values as std::string
literals, which lacks type safety and can lead to typos or invalid values
that are only caught at runtime.

The resource.hpp header already defines State and Health enums with proper
NLOHMANN_JSON_SERIALIZE_ENUM mappings, used extensively throughout the
codebase (120+ locations). However, some utility functions still return
strings instead of using these enums.

This commit converts the following functions and variables to use type-safe
enums:
- sensor_utils::getHealth() return type: string -> resource::Health
- sw_utils::getRedfishSwHealth() return type: string -> resource::Health  
- Local State and Health variables in processor.hpp and sensors.hpp
- State assignments in event_service.hpp

Benefits:
- Compile-time type checking prevents invalid values
- Better IDE support with auto-completion
- Consistent with existing codebase patterns
- No functional changes - enums serialize to identical JSON strings

Tested: Verified CI passes with no compilation errors or warnings
Signed-off-by: Vinothkumar S <your.email@example.com>

```

```
Use enums for State and Health properties

Several utility functions return State and Health values as
std::string literals, which lacks compile-time type safety.
This can lead to typos or invalid values that are only caught
at runtime.

Convert these functions to return resource::State and
resource::Health enums instead. These enums are already
defined in resource.hpp with NLOHMANN_JSON_SERIALIZE_ENUM
mappings and are used extensively throughout the codebase.

The enums automatically serialize to the same JSON strings, so
there is no functional change. This provides compile-time type
checking.

Tested:
- No functional change.
- Verified State and Health properties serialize to identical
  JSON values.

Change-Id: I590fc3dddac6f126c26814b549d2fea961409170
Signed-off-by: Vinothkumar Shanmugavel <vinothkumars@ami.com>

```
</details></tool-use>

```
commit 793f6891ca17db27ea8f4c45ef80bba6dccda034
Author: Vinothkumar Shanmugavel <vinothkumars@ami.com>
Commit: Ed Tanous <ed@tanous.net>

    systems: Prevent empty UUID and SubModel
    
    The afterGetUUID and afterGetInventory handlers set UUID and
    SubModel properties without validating D-Bus returned values are
    non-empty. Per Redfish schema, UUID must be a valid RFC4122
    identifier and empty strings are invalid. This adds empty string
    checks to prevent setting invalid property values in the Redfish
    response.
    
    When D-Bus returns empty strings for these properties (which can
    occur during early boot or with certain hardware configurations),
    they will now be omitted from the response rather than returned
    as empty values.
    
    Tested:
    - Verified properties are omitted when D-Bus returns empty string
    - Verified properties are correctly set when valid values present
    - No functional change when valid non-empty values are returned
    
    Change-Id: I80b4f8588cb065d25097f4fd3712987adef820c0
    Signed-off-by: Vinothkumar Shanmugavel <vinothkumars@ami.com>
```
</details></tool-use>

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
Great questions!

## 1. Why if-elif without else is not a problem:

The key is the **initialization**. Look at line 645:

```cpp
resource::Health health = resource::Health::Critical;
```

The variable is initialized to `Critical` by default, so:
- If `status->ends_with("Full")` → health becomes `OK`
- Else if `status->ends_with("Degraded")` → health becomes `Warning`
- **Else (any other case)** → health stays `Critical` (the default)

This is actually **better design** than having an else block because:
- ✅ Variable is always initialized (satisfies clang-tidy)
- ✅ Default case is explicit (Critical)
- ✅ Less code, more readable
- ✅ Handles unexpected status values safely

Great questions!

## 1. Why if-elif without else is not a problem:

The key is the **initialization**. Look at line 645:

```cpp
resource::Health health = resource::Health::Critical;
```

The variable is initialized to  by default, so:
- If  → health becomes 
- Else if  → health becomes 
- **Else (any other case)** → health stays  (the default)

This is actually **better design** than having an else block because:
- ✅ Variable is always initialized (satisfies clang-tidy)
- ✅ Default case is explicit (Critical)
- ✅ Less code, more readable
- ✅ Handles unexpected status values safely
